messages.subject: Shore Based Counts Using ONLY ONE LINE TRANSECT
messages.subject_clean: Shore Based Counts Using ONLY ONE LINE TRANSECT
messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone,

I am a masters student course work student and new to distance sampling.  I
am undertaking a small research project involving the use of distance
sampling from a shore based platform to estimate daily densities of
migratory humpback whales.

Having read applicable sections of the Distance text in relation to
line transects and other articles regarding measurements of distance from
shore for migratory whales, I find that I still need some clarification on
several points as to obtaining distance measurements with respect using
line transects.

Since the whales will be passing a stationary point (coming from the same
direction) is it more appropriate to use a =93one-sided=94 line transect in
which the width is undefined for the one side of the transect? Then take
distance measurements as the whale groups approach some pre-defined
centreline (maybe defined by a degree measurement)?  (Survey area would be
defined by the field of view from initial detection southernmost point to
the centreline)

Other articles I have read in relation to distance measurements and shore
based counts only describe that measurements were taken when whale groups
were approximately in line with the counting station.  However, it is
unclear what is meant by =93approximate=94 or how this width of the transect=

from a centreline was defined.

Would it be more appropriate to define widths on either side of the
centreline of the line transect to collect distance data? Only doing this
would cause the widths to be extremely wide and that does not appear to be
correct.

Thank you in advance for assistance.

messages.subject_clean: Shore Based Counts Using ONLY ONE LINE TRANSECT
messages.body_plain:
Lisa, line transect methods are inappropriate for land-based surveys of
humpback whales.  The animals are not uniformly distributed with respect
to distance from the shore.  Put another way, you don't have a large
number of lines, positioned randomly with respect to the whales.  Take a
look at the section on 'migration counts' in the 1993 distance sampling
book (which is on the RUWPA web page - see below).

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: naturally truncated distances
messages.body_plain:
> > I'm working on my Master's project doing density estimates of cavity nestings birds with the line transect methods.  Transects are placed in forest stands that are delineated by GIS.  The stands very in size and shape and are in one of 4 strata based on cover type and size classes.  I'm working in an area in which forest stands are often surrounded by expanses of grassland (Blue Mts. NE Oregon).  Therefore, outside of the stand is nonhabitat for cavity nesters and detections are impossible beyond the boundaries of the stand.  My question is how this situation will turn out in the analysis.  For example, in large stands where the distance on either side of my transect in which I can detect a woodpecker is unlimited, the detection function for some of these species is quite great.  However, in some of these narrow stands where I can see the edge as close as 50 m away,  the ability to detect the same birds is only as great as that distance.  I've been trying to lay transects
  !
pe!
> > rpendicular to these edges.  Is this the right solution?  Should the data be treated differently when the distance from the transect to the edge is close? You can send a reply to me personally at :nssa...@yahoo.com or to the whole group if you prefer.  I only have access to email about once a week.  Thanks for any advice.Nicole Seaman

This issue is discussed on pp214-6 of the 2001 distance sampling book (see
the RUWPA web page below for info - click on 'publications').  It will be
discussed in greater detail in the advanced volume, which is due to go to
the publishers soon.  A simple solution to the problem is to define a grid
of lines over the survey area, where the survey area has a 'bufferzone'
extending a distance w beyond the habitat, where w is the maximum
detection distance from the line.  Then survey the line segments in the
bufferzone as well as those in the trees.  With random placement of the
grid of lines (and sufficient lines - say 15 or more), this ensures a
uniform distribution of objects with respect to distance from the line.
Thus the short detection distances recorded from lines running through
small patches of trees are offset by relatively large distances recorded
from lines passing close to, but outside, patches of trees.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hi Werner,

> >1. When I select a model definition it has to be typed additionally into 2
> >other windows (in these windows there is no option of selecting models). How
> >can I be sure that the computer analyses the model first selected (then the
> >name typed somewhere else instead of being selected) and not another model?
> >During further analyses it also keeps on using the first model.

The Model Definition selected for an analysis is the one highlighted under
"Model Definition" in the Analysis Details Inputs tab.  If you want to change
the name of the Model Definition you can either type in a new name there, or
click on "Properties..." and type in a new name in the Model Definition
Properties window.

I suggest you carefully read the online manual Chapter 7.  This explains the
difference between an Analysis and a Model Definition, which is something people
often get confused about.  Under "Working with Data Filters and Model
Definitions" it explains how to select a Model Definition for an analysis.

One of these days I'll get around to completing the getting started pages to
include an example analysis, which will hopefully make life easier for
beginners.

> >2. Why does the program forces me to ignore data collected on the line, i.e.
> >on 0 meters? Shouldn't this data be included in the analysis?

It doesn't force you to ignore this data.  The default left truncation is "No
truncation" for exact data, and when you have interval data, the default lowest
cutpoint of 0 includes distances at 0.  This latter point is documented in the
online manual (select the Data Filter | Intervals tab, press F1 and read the
Aside at the bottom of the page).

> >3. We surveyed 8 lines counting francolins in distance intervals. The terrain
> >did not allow for long lines. We therefore monitored 8 short lines (+- 800m
> >each), but individual lines did not produce sufficiently large numbers that
> >warrant individual analyses. We then pooled the data from the 8 lines (218
> >francolins in total). To estimate variation, should the pooled data (8 lines)
> >be bootstrapped, OR should density be estimated for each line separately and
> >then variation calculated?

I'm not sure exactly what you did here.  Assuming you have each line in Distance
as a separate record in the sample layer (probably called "Line transect" in
your project), then I assume you asked in the Model Definition for a global
density estimate and global encounter rate, which is why you say you "pooled"
the data from the 8 lines.  To estimate variance, use the default method, under
the Variance tab in Model definition, which is to estimate variance empirically.
How this is done is detailed in the Distance Sampling book (Introduction to
Distance Sampling pages 78-89; or you can get a copy of the previous edition
from the Distance web site). If you want to bootstrap, you can bootstrap by
sample in the Variance tab.  However, 8 lines is very few for a reliable
empirical estimate of variance, and really too few for a reliable bootstrap.
For that you would ideally want at least 20-30 lines, with good spatial coverage
(see the survey design chapter in the book).

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

On Mon, 19 May 2003 10:47:08 -0700, Rodney Siegel wrote:

> >Distance samplers,

> >I want to run an analysis in Distance 4 in which I estimate a detection
> >function for a relatively frequently detected 'surrogate' species, and then
> >apply that detection function to a rarer species which likely has a similar
> >detectability function (based on similar vocalizations, behavior,
> >etc.).  What's the best way to set this up?  I should add that I want to
> >fit a global detection function for the surrogate species (because I have
> >no reason to think detectability should vary across the study site), but I
> >need stratum-specific density estimates for the rare species (because
> >density surely varies across the site).  My first idea was to use the data
> >filter to combine data for the surrogate species and the rare species, and
> >then to post-stratify on species name... but this precludes producing
> >density estimates specific to the real strata-- which are defined
> >geographically.

> >Thanks for any help anyone can provide!

> >******************************************
> >Rodney Siegel
> >The Institute for Bird Populations
> >P.O. Box 1346
> >Point Reyes Station, CA 94956-1346
> >tel:(415) 663-2051
> >fax:(415) 663-9482
> >email: rsi...@birdpop.org
> >web: www.birdpop.org <http://www.birdpop.org>

In any case, I guess I'm best placed to answer your question, but I'm forwarding
my reply to the list as it's quite a common question.

Look in the online help, under Multipliers in the Index.  At the bottom of that
page, under "Additional uses of multipliers" it shows you how to do exactly what
you want, which is to use a multiplier to specify the probability of detection
for the rarer species, basing the probability on that estimated from the common
species.  The only downside of this approach is that you can't then use the
bootstrap to estimate variance for the rarer species, as the multiplier SE is
not used during the bootstrap (see online help Appendix - Program Reference,
Model Definition Properties, Multipliers).  A minor inconvenience though.

Cheers,

 - Len

messages.body_plain:
Hmmm - sneaky!  Great idea Jeff.

This will include both the surrogate and rarer species in the detection function
estimation, where the multiplier approach I suggested could use only the surrogate
species or both species, depending on how you specify data selection in the
detection function analysis.

The big advantage of Jeff's approach is that you can do the whole thing in one
analysis, rather than the two that mine would take.

You could also have a go at bootstrap variance estimation with Jeff's approach,
but the results wouldn't be strictly correct as you'd want to resample by transect
and when a transect is picked that should include the transect from the "surrogate
species stratum" and that same transect in the "rarer species strata".  (You could
do slightly better by having the original strata with area 0 for surrogate
species, and repeating the strata with true area for the rare species -- at least
you'll be resampling transects within strata then, even if the transects for
surrogate and rare species are still not matched.)  I shouldn't think it'll create
a huge bias in variance estimate in practice however, especially since variance of
f(0) estimate is usually a small component of variance in D.

 - Len

messages.subject: Re: Two Belt Methods
messages.body_plain:
> >     I'm analyzing some transect data obtained with the two belt method.
> > Birds deteected were classified just as within 25 m of distance or out
> > of this band.

For point transects, this is given on p204-5 of the 2001 distance
sampling book.  (It's also in the 1993 book.)  The maths doesn't work out
so nicely for line transects - see the reference to Jarvinen and Vaisanen
on p206.  For the half-normal model, you have to use numerical methods, so
the easy solution is to use Distance with 2 distance bands, giving some
upper limit for the outer band.  100m might work OK for smaller species -
try different choices, based on estimates of the maximum distance a
species is potentially detectable, and see if estimation is sensitive to
this choice.

Steve Buckland
